why_how.text: Sign shapes and colors are coded so you understand a sign before you can read it, and the colors follow national standards.

scenario.text: Far ahead, Jo sees an orange sign but cannot yet read its words.

reasoning.text: On warning signs, orange warns and controls in construction zones.

result.text: Jo slows down and expects a construction zone before she can read the sign.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking yellow-green signs mean the same as orange signs.

correction.text: Yellow-green is limited to pedestrian and bicycle crossings and school areas, while orange is the color of construction zones.

memory_support.text: Red and white rule, yellow warns, yellow-green for crossings, orange for work, green, blue and brown guide.

prompt.text: What does a brown informational sign mark?

rationale.text: Green guides and informs, blue describes motorist services, and brown marks historic, cultural or recreational sites.

narration.text: Minnesota's signs, signals and pavement markings follow national standards, so the same colors and shapes mean the same thing across the country. This unit explains how that coding works. Sign shapes and colors are coded so that you can grasp a sign's general meaning before you are close enough to read it. You will learn the colors used on regulatory, warning and informational signs, the seven common shapes the manual names, and why some warning signs appear in fluorescent yellow-green. Once the color code is second nature, every sign starts telling you something from far away.

Road signs combine uniform symbols and pictures with written instructions. Besides colors, the manual names seven common sign shapes: octagon, triangle, diamond, rectangle, pentagon, crossbuck and circle. Sign shapes and colors are coded so that you can grasp a sign's general meaning before you are close enough to read it. In practice, that means the color and outline of a sign give you a first message from a distance, and the symbols and words fill in the details as you get closer. Learning both layers lets you react sooner.

On regulatory signs, red prohibits and commands, while white regulates. On warning signs, yellow warns, yellow-green warns and controls at pedestrian and bicycle crossings and school areas, and orange warns and controls in construction zones. Most warning signs are yellow, but pedestrian crossing, bicycle crossing and school zone signs may be yellow or fluorescent yellow-green. So red and white tell you what you must or must not do, while yellow, yellow-green and orange tell you what to watch out for, with yellow-green and orange each pointing to a specific kind of place.

Here is the trap. Yellow and yellow-green both warn, but yellow-green is limited to pedestrian and bicycle crossings and school areas, while orange is the color of construction zones. Some drivers treat any bright warning color as the same thing. They are not the same. A fluorescent yellow-green sign points to people crossing or a school nearby, so think children, walkers and bicyclists. An orange sign points to road work, so think workers, equipment and changed lanes. Reading the exact color tells you what kind of hazard to expect ahead.

On informational signs, green guides and informs, blue describes motorist services, and brown marks historic, cultural or recreational sites. These colors do not order you to do anything. Instead, they help you find your way. Green shows you where you are going, blue shows you where to stop for services you may need, and brown points you toward places worth visiting. Together with the regulatory and warning colors, they complete the color code. A driver who knows all of them can read the purpose of almost any sign before the words come into view.

Here is a quick check: what does a brown informational sign mark? Recall the informational colors. On informational signs, green guides and informs, blue describes motorist services, and brown marks historic, cultural or recreational sites. So the answer is historic, cultural or recreational sites. That separates brown from blue, which points to services, and green, which guides you along your route. Remember that the colors are coded so you can grasp a sign's general meaning before you are close enough to read it, which is exactly when the color helps most.

To sum up, Minnesota's signs follow national standards, combining symbols and pictures with words, in seven common shapes from octagon to circle. Shapes and colors are coded so you understand a sign before you can read it. Red prohibits and commands and white regulates. Yellow warns, yellow-green covers pedestrian and bicycle crossings and school areas, and orange covers construction zones, with most warning signs yellow. Green guides and informs, blue describes motorist services, and brown marks historic, cultural or recreational sites.

why_how.text: Regulatory signs are laws you must obey, and ignoring one can bring a citation and a fine.
Several regulatory signs look alike in purpose but require different actions.

scenario.text: At an intersection, Max has a Yield sign while cross traffic has no sign, and no cars are coming.

reasoning.text: At a Yield sign, slow down or stop if necessary and give the right-of-way to all other vehicles and pedestrians until it is safe.

result.text: Max slows, sees no traffic or pedestrians, and continues without a full stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a Yield sign always requires a full stop.

correction.text: A Yield sign requires stopping only if necessary to give the right-of-way, while a Stop sign always requires a full stop.

memory_support.text: Stop means stop, yield means give way, slash means don't.

prompt.text: On a controlled-access interstate with a posted minimum speed, when may you drive below the minimum?

answer.text: Only when bad weather or poor road conditions require it.

rationale.text: Speed limit signs show the maximum, and freeway minimums must not be undercut in normal conditions.

lines.text: Do Not Enter and Wrong Way

narration.text: Regulatory signs require you to follow traffic laws, and ignoring one can bring a traffic citation and a fine. This unit covers the most common ones: the Stop sign, the Yield sign, the Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs, the red circle with a slash, speed limit and minimum speed signs, and the signs that mark no-passing zones. Several pairs look similar in purpose but call for different actions, so the unit points them out. If you know exactly what each regulatory sign requires, you can obey it without hesitation and avoid a ticket.

lines.text: Stop: full stop, wait, then go
Yield: slow or stop if needed
Give way to vehicles and pedestrians

narration.text: At a Stop sign, come to a full stop and wait until every pedestrian and vehicle that has the right-of-way is out of the intersection, then go on with caution. At a Yield sign, slow down or stop if necessary and give the right-of-way to all other vehicles and pedestrians until it is safe to go. The difference is in the stop. A Stop sign always requires one. A Yield sign requires one only if you must stop to give the right-of-way. Both signs mean other people may have the right to go first. To restate the key point: At a Yield sign, slow down or stop if necessary and give the right-of-way to all other vehicles and pedestrians until it is safe to go.

title.text: Do Not Enter and Wrong Way

lines.text: Do Not Enter facing you: stay out
Wrong Way: you are against traffic
Red circle and slash: not allowed

narration.text: A Do Not Enter sign facing you means you may not enter that lane or road. A Wrong Way sign means you have entered a lane of oncoming traffic and are traveling in the wrong direction. A red circle with a red slash across a symbol, as on No Left Turn, No Right Turn, No U Turn and No Parking signs, means the action shown is not allowed. If you ever see a Wrong Way sign facing you, you are already in danger, and you need to leave that lane as soon as you can do so safely. Put simply: A Do Not Enter sign facing you means you may not enter that lane or road.

lines.text: Do Not Enter: before you go in
Wrong Way: you are already in

narration.text: Here is the trap. A Do Not Enter sign facing you forbids going into that lane or road, while a Wrong Way sign means you are already in a lane of oncoming traffic. They are not two ways of saying the same thing. Do Not Enter is the warning before the mistake, at the point where you could still choose not to turn in. Wrong Way is the warning after the mistake, telling you that you have already entered against traffic. A question may ask which sign tells you that you have gone the wrong way; the answer is Wrong Way. Remember this rule: A Do Not Enter sign facing you means you may not enter that lane or road.

lines.text: Do Not Pass marks a no-passing zone

narration.text: A speed limit sign shows the maximum speed for the road, and controlled-access interstate freeways may also post minimum limits that you must not go below unless bad weather or poor road conditions require it. The regulatory Do Not Pass sign marks where a no-passing zone begins. Two different signs mark a no-passing zone: the regulatory Do Not Pass sign, and the No Passing Zone warning sign placed on the left side of a two-way highway at the start of the zone. Either one tells you that passing is no longer allowed from that point.

lines.text: No Passing Zone on the left side

narration.text: The two no-passing signs are a common source of confusion because they come from different groups. The Do Not Pass sign is regulatory, and it marks where a no-passing zone begins. The No Passing Zone sign is a warning sign, and it is placed on the left side of a two-way highway at the start of the zone. Two different signs mark a no-passing zone, but they share one message: do not pass from here on. When you see either one, finish any pass you have started and stay behind the vehicle ahead. Once more: The regulatory Do Not Pass sign marks where a no-passing zone begins.

Here is a quick check: you are driving on a controlled-access interstate freeway that posts a minimum speed. When may you drive below that minimum? Recall the speed sign rule. A speed limit sign shows the maximum speed for the road, and controlled-access interstate freeways may also post minimum limits that you must not go below unless bad weather or poor road conditions require it. So the answer is only when bad weather or poor road conditions make a lower speed necessary. In normal conditions, stay at or above the posted minimum and at or below the posted maximum.

lines.text: Do Not Enter versus Wrong Way

narration.text: To finish, regulatory signs require you to follow traffic laws, and ignoring one can bring a citation and a fine. At a Stop sign, stop fully and wait for those with the right-of-way; at a Yield sign, slow or stop if needed and give way. Do Not Enter keeps you out of a lane or road, and Wrong Way tells you that you are already in oncoming traffic. A red circle with a slash forbids the action shown. Speed limit signs show the maximum, freeways may post minimums, and both the Do Not Pass sign and the No Passing Zone sign mark a no-passing zone.

why_how.text: Lane signs tell you where to be before you turn, and parking signs reserve spaces for those who need them.
Some lane signs apply to traffic from both directions at once.

scenario.text: Rosa approaches a multilane roundabout, wanting to turn right, and sees lane signs posted ahead.

reasoning.text: Before a multilane roundabout, signs show which lane to use for each turn, so move into the correct lane well in advance, such as the right lane only to turn right.

result.text: Rosa moves into the right lane early and turns right at the roundabout.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a center lane marked left-turn only belongs to traffic in one direction.

correction.text: Traffic from both directions shares the center lane and may use it only to make left turns.

memory_support.text: Arrow shows the one way, keep right of islands, pick roundabout lanes early, diamonds are reserved.

prompt.text: The designated disability spaces are full. What may a driver with a valid disability permit do?

answer.text: Park at an angle across two standard spaces.

rationale.text: Only vehicles with disability plates or a permit may use the blue-signed spaces, and when they are full, angle parking across two spaces is allowed.

narration.text: This unit covers signs that tell you where to place your vehicle. You will learn the One Way and Keep Right signs, how roundabout lane signs work, lane-use control signs, the No Turn on Red sign, the center lane left-turn only sign, the Reduced Speed Ahead sign, the diamond symbol for reserved lanes, and the rules for disability parking spaces. Many of these signs appear before you need to act, so the skill is reading them early and moving into the right position in time. A late lane change near a turn is exactly what these signs help you avoid.

lines.text: Keep Right: stay right of the island

narration.text: A One Way sign means traffic in that lane moves only in the direction of the arrow. A Keep Right sign tells you to stay to the right of a traffic island, median or obstruction ahead. A Reduced Speed Ahead sign means a lower speed limit is coming, so begin slowing down. Each of these signs gives you advance notice of a change in where or how fast you should drive. Following the arrow, keeping right of the island and easing off before the new limit all happen before you reach the spot the sign warns about. To restate the key point: A One Way sign means traffic in that lane moves only in the direction of the arrow.

lines.text: Signs show the lane for each turn
Choose the lane well in advance
Right lane right, left lane left

narration.text: Before a multilane roundabout, signs show which lane to use for each turn, so move into the correct lane well in advance, for example the right lane only to turn right and the left lane only to turn left. In the multilane roundabout sign example, going straight is allowed from either lane even though turning right and turning left are each limited to one lane. Choosing your lane early matters because inside the roundabout you should not change lanes. Read the lane signs on the approach and settle into the right lane before you reach the yield line.

lines.text: No Turn on Red: wait for green

narration.text: A lane-use control sign means you must turn if you are in the lane it marks, though a sign may also show that one lane can go straight or turn. A No Turn on Red sign means you wait for a green signal before turning. A center lane left-turn only sign means traffic from both directions shares the center lane and may use it only to make left turns. So if you find yourself in a marked turn lane, you turn. If a No Turn on Red sign is posted, you wait for green. And the shared center lane is only for left turns. Put simply: A No Turn on Red sign means you wait for a green signal before turning.

Here is the trap. Some drivers treat a center lane marked left-turn only as their own lane, or as a place to pass slow traffic. Neither is correct. Traffic from both directions shares the center lane and may use it only to make left turns. That means a driver coming the other way may be in the same lane, waiting to turn left too. Enter the center lane only to make your left turn, and watch for oncoming drivers who are also using it. It is never a passing lane or a lane for driving any distance. Remember this rule: A center lane left-turn only sign means traffic from both directions shares the center lane and may use it only to make left turns.

lines.text: Blue sign: plates or permit only

narration.text: A diamond symbol marks a lane reserved for certain uses or vehicles, such as cars with two or more passengers, buses, commercial vehicles or bicycles. Only vehicles carrying disability license plates or a disability parking permit may use spaces marked with blue disability parking signs. If the designated disability spaces are full or unavailable, a driver with a valid disability permit or plates may park at an angle across two standard spaces. These rules reserve space for the people who need it, whether that is a carpool lane or a parking spot near the door.

Here is a quick check: a driver with a valid disability permit arrives to find every designated disability space full. What may the driver do? Recall the parking rule. Only vehicles carrying disability license plates or a disability parking permit may use spaces marked with blue disability parking signs. If those designated spaces are full or unavailable, a driver with a valid disability permit or plates may park at an angle across two standard spaces. So the answer is to park at an angle across two standard spaces, which gives the extra room the driver may need.

lines.text: One Way, Keep Right, Reduced Speed
Roundabout lanes, turn lanes, center lane

narration.text: To recap, a One Way sign means follow the arrow, Keep Right means stay right of an island or obstruction, and Reduced Speed Ahead means start slowing. Before a multilane roundabout, pick your lane early from the signs; in the example straight is allowed from either lane. A lane-use control sign means you must turn from a marked lane, No Turn on Red means wait for green, and a center left-turn lane is shared by both directions for left turns only. Diamonds mark reserved lanes, and blue disability spaces are for plates or permits, with angle parking across two spaces when they are full.

why_how.text: Signs near railroads, schools and crosswalks protect people who cannot stop or get out of the way quickly.
The exempt sign changes the usual stop for buses and trucks.

scenario.text: A school bus driver approaches a railroad crossing marked with a crossbuck and an exempt sign.

reasoning.text: An exempt sign lets bus and truck drivers who normally must stop go on without stopping, though they must still look both ways for trains.

result.text: The bus driver continues without stopping but looks both ways for trains.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an exempt sign means no one needs to look for trains.

correction.text: Even under an exempt sign, bus and truck drivers must still look both ways for trains.

memory_support.text: Stop line, X and RR on the road; crossbuck counts tracks; pentagon means school.

prompt.text: A crossing has two tracks. Where does the crossbuck tell you that?

answer.text: A sign below the crossbuck shows how many tracks there are.

rationale.text: An X-shaped crossbuck marks a railroad crossing, and a sign below it shows the number of tracks when there is more than one.

narration.text: Some of the most important warning signs protect people near railroads, schools and crosswalks. This unit covers the pavement markings painted before a railroad crossing, the crossbuck and the sign that shows how many tracks there are, the exempt sign, railroad crossing ahead signs, the pentagon-shaped school zone sign, the school crossing sign, the pedestrian crossing sign, and the arrow plaque that accompanies crossing signs. Each one tells you to slow down and get ready to stop, and some tell you exactly who may continue and who may not.

lines.text: Stop line, X and RR on the road

narration.text: Pavement markings in front of a railroad crossing include a stop line, an X and the letters RR. An X-shaped crossbuck sign marks a railroad crossing, and when there is more than one track, a sign below it shows how many. Railroad crossing ahead signs mean slow down, look carefully both ways and be ready to stop, because trains cannot stop quickly. So you get warnings in layers: a sign ahead, markings on the road, and the crossbuck at the tracks. Each layer is a reminder to slow down and look both ways. Once more: Pavement markings in front of a railroad crossing include a stop line, an X and the letters RR.

lines.text: Buses and trucks may skip the stop
They must still look both ways

narration.text: Here is the trap. An exempt sign at a railroad crossing lets bus and truck drivers who normally must stop go on without stopping, though they must still look both ways for trains. Some people read exempt as meaning the crossing is safe or the rules do not apply. That is wrong. The exempt sign changes only the required stop for buses and trucks. It does not remove the duty to look for trains, and it does not change anything for the train. Every driver at every crossing still checks both directions before going on. To restate the key point: An X-shaped crossbuck sign marks a railroad crossing, and when there is more than one track, a sign below it shows how many.

lines.text: Watch for children, be ready to stop

narration.text: Pentagon-shaped school zone signs, yellow or fluorescent yellow-green, warn that a school or an approved school crosswalk is ahead, so watch for children and be ready to stop. At a school crossing sign, watch for children and be ready to stop, since drivers must yield to every pedestrian in a crosswalk. The school crossing and pedestrian crossing signs each come with an arrow sign below them, which the manual calls the standard marking. The pentagon shape is a strong clue on its own: when you see it, think school, and slow down.

lines.text: Slow down and be ready to stop

narration.text: A pedestrian crossing sign means slow down, be ready to stop, and yield to pedestrians crossing at intersections and crosswalks. As with the school crossing sign, the pedestrian crossing sign comes with an arrow sign below it, which the manual calls the standard marking. The arrow points to the crossing location. These signs work together with the yielding rules you have already learned: pedestrians in a crosswalk have the right-of-way, and your job is to slow down early enough that you can stop smoothly if someone steps out.

Here is a quick check: how does a crossbuck show that a railroad crossing has more than one track? Recall the railroad sign rules. An X-shaped crossbuck sign marks a railroad crossing, and when there is more than one track, a sign below it shows how many. So the answer is a sign below the crossbuck. Knowing the number of tracks matters, because more than one train may approach from different directions. Pavement markings before the crossing, including a stop line, an X and the letters RR, add another warning. Put simply: Pavement markings in front of a railroad crossing include a stop line, an X and the letters RR.

lines.text: Exempt: skip the stop, still look

narration.text: To wrap up, pavement markings before a railroad crossing include a stop line, an X and RR, a crossbuck marks the crossing, and a sign below it shows how many tracks there are. Railroad crossing ahead signs mean slow, look both ways and be ready to stop. An exempt sign lets buses and trucks skip the usual stop, but they still look both ways. Pentagon school zone signs warn of a school or school crosswalk, school and pedestrian crossing signs mean slow, be ready to stop and yield, and both carry the arrow plaque the manual calls the standard marking.

why_how.text: Warning signs tell you about the road ahead before you can see it, so you have time to slow and position yourself.
Slow vehicles and intersection shapes call for specific responses.

scenario.text: On a rural road, Ben sees a sign warning that the road splits ahead into two directions.

reasoning.text: A Y-intersection sign means the road splits in two directions, so expect crossing traffic and get ready to bear one way or the other.

result.text: Ben slows, watches for crossing traffic, and prepares to bear toward his route.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a T-intersection sign and a Y-intersection sign as the same warning.

correction.text: At a T your road ends, so you turn and yield to cross traffic, while at a Y the road splits into two directions.

memory_support.text: Emblem means thirty or slower, T ends, Y splits, curve speed is the speed.

prompt.text: What does a two-way traffic ahead sign tell you?

answer.text: You are leaving a one-way road for a two-way road, so stay right.

rationale.text: It warns that oncoming traffic will share the road ahead.

narration.text: Warning signs give you time. They tell you about a slow vehicle, an intersection or a change in the road before you reach it, so you can slow down and choose your position calmly. This unit covers the slow-moving vehicle emblem and animal-drawn vehicles, the crossroad, side road, T-intersection and Y-intersection signs, curve signs with posted speeds, roundabout warnings, winding road and road turns signs, two-way traffic and divided highway signs, and the traffic signal ahead sign. Some of these pairs look alike in purpose but warn of quite different situations.

lines.text: Lamp at night visible five hundred feet

narration.text: The slow-moving vehicle emblem must be shown on every vehicle traveling thirty mph or less on a public road, such as farm implements or animal-drawn vehicles, so adjust your speed or get ready to change lanes when you see it. Slow down and pass animal-drawn vehicles slowly; from sunset to sunrise or in poor visibility they must carry a light or lamp visible within five hundred feet. When you see the emblem, expect a big speed difference, slow down early and pass only when it is safe to do so. Remember this rule: Slow down and pass animal-drawn vehicles slowly; from sunset to sunrise or in poor visibility they must carry a light or lamp visible within five hundred feet.

lines.text: Side road: traffic from the right

narration.text: A crossroad sign means an intersection is ahead and you should prepare to yield. A side road sign means traffic is coming from your right, so watch for vehicles entering the road. A T-intersection ahead sign means your road ends soon, so get ready to turn right or left and yield to cross traffic. A Y-intersection sign means the road splits in two directions, so expect crossing traffic and get ready to bear one way or the other. Each sign gives you a picture of the intersection before you arrive. Once more: A crossroad sign means an intersection is ahead and you should prepare to yield.

Here is a trap. The T-intersection and Y-intersection signs both mean your road is about to change, but in different ways. A T-intersection ahead sign means your road ends soon, so get ready to turn right or left and yield to cross traffic. A Y-intersection sign means the road splits in two directions, so expect crossing traffic and get ready to bear one way or the other. At a T you must turn and yield, because your road stops. At a Y you choose a branch, still watching for traffic crossing your path. To restate the key point: A T-intersection ahead sign means your road ends soon, so get ready to turn right or left and yield to cross traffic.

If a curve sign shows a speed, slow to that speed for the curve. A roundabout warning sign means slow to the advisory speed as you approach and be ready to stop. A winding road sign means the road bends back and forth ahead, while a road turns ahead sign means it changes direction sharply; slow down for both. A traffic signal ahead sign warns that the next intersection has a traffic light. In every case the sign asks for a lower speed or a readiness to stop, and the earlier you respond, the smoother the change will be. Put simply: If a curve sign shows a speed, slow to that speed for the curve.

A two-way traffic ahead sign means you are leaving a one-way road for a two-way road, so stay to the right. A divided highway begins sign tells you to stay right as the road divides, while a divided highway ends sign warns that two-way traffic will no longer be separated by a center island. These signs all deal with how opposing traffic will be arranged ahead. When the center island ends or a one-way road becomes two-way, oncoming vehicles will be closer to you, so keeping right becomes even more important. Remember this rule: A two-way traffic ahead sign means you are leaving a one-way road for a two-way road, so stay to the right.

Here is a quick check: what does a two-way traffic ahead sign tell you? Recall the road arrangement signs. A two-way traffic ahead sign means you are leaving a one-way road for a two-way road, so stay to the right. That differs from a divided highway ends sign, which warns that two-way traffic will no longer be separated by a center island. Both signs mean oncoming traffic will soon share the road more closely with you. In both cases you keep to the right and watch for vehicles coming toward you. Once more: A two-way traffic ahead sign means you are leaving a one-way road for a two-way road, so stay to the right.

lines.text: Crossroad, side road, T and Y

narration.text: To finish, the slow-moving vehicle emblem marks vehicles going thirty mph or less, and animal-drawn vehicles need a lamp visible within five hundred feet at night. A crossroad sign means prepare to yield, a side road sign means traffic from the right, a T means your road ends and you yield, and a Y means the road splits. Slow to a posted curve speed, slow to the advisory speed at a roundabout, and slow for winding roads and sharp turns. Keep right when two-way traffic begins or a divided highway ends, and expect a light after a traffic signal ahead sign.

why_how.text: Hazard signs warn of surfaces, slopes and lane changes that can catch you by surprise.
Three merge-related signs ask for three different actions.

scenario.text: On a highway, Cara's right lane is about to end and a lane ends sign appears.

reasoning.text: A lane ends sign means two lanes are becoming one, and in the example shown the right-lane vehicles must yield and merge into the left lane.

result.text: Cara signals, yields to traffic in the left lane and merges when there is a gap.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an added lane sign means new traffic must merge.

correction.text: With an added lane sign the new traffic does not need to merge at all.

memory_support.text: Lane ends yields, merging makes room, added lane needs no merge.

prompt.text: You drive a tall truck toward an overpass marked with a low clearance sign lower than your truck. What should you do?

answer.text: Do not go on; the vehicle may become stuck.

rationale.text: A vehicle taller than the posted height may become stuck.

narration.text: This unit covers warning signs about the road itself. Some warn of things that may cross your path, some warn of slippery surfaces or steep grades, and some warn that lanes are about to change. The three lane signs, lane ends, merging traffic and added lane, each ask for a different action, so the unit compares them directly. Finally you will see the low clearance and narrow bridge signs, which warn of tight spaces ahead. Responding to these signs early is what keeps a surprise from turning into a crash. To restate the key point: Crossing signs warn you to watch for animals, people or vehicles crossing the road.

Crossing signs warn you to watch for animals, people or vehicles crossing the road. A slippery road sign warns that the surface is slippery when wet and is often placed near bridges and overpasses. A steep hill sign means the road drops sharply ahead, so be sure your brakes work before you go on. Each of these signs asks for more caution than the road might seem to need at first glance. Slow down where crossings are marked, ease off on wet surfaces near bridges, and check your brakes before a steep descent. Put simply: Crossing signs warn you to watch for animals, people or vehicles crossing the road.

lines.text: In the example, right lane yields

narration.text: A lane ends sign means two lanes are becoming one, and in the example shown the right-lane vehicles must yield and merge into the left lane. The driver in the ending lane carries the duty to yield. Watch the sign as you approach and merge when there is a safe gap in the lane that continues. Drivers already in the continuing lane do not have to stop for you, so plan your merge before the lane runs out rather than at the very end. Remember this rule: A lane ends sign means two lanes are becoming one, and in the example shown the right-lane vehicles must yield and merge into the left lane.

Here is the trap. With a lane ends sign the ending lane must yield and merge, with a merging traffic sign you make room for vehicles joining your road, and with an added lane sign the new traffic does not need to merge at all. These three signs look related, and drivers often mix up who must act. The lane ends sign puts the duty on the ending lane. The merging traffic sign asks you to help others join. The added lane sign means a new lane begins, so no one has to merge into anyone. Once more: A lane ends sign means two lanes are becoming one, and in the example shown the right-lane vehicles must yield and merge into the left lane.

lines.text: Low clearance: too tall, do not go

narration.text: A low clearance sign means you must not go on if your vehicle is taller than the height shown, or it may become stuck. A narrow bridge sign means the bridge ahead is narrower than the road leading to it. Both signs warn of a space that is smaller than you might expect. If you drive a tall vehicle, such as a moving truck, check the height on the sign before you reach the overpass. At a narrow bridge, slow down and watch for oncoming traffic that will be closer to you than on the road before it. To restate the key point: A narrow bridge sign means the bridge ahead is narrower than the road leading to it.

Here is a quick check: you are driving a tall moving truck, and a low clearance sign shows a height lower than your vehicle. What should you do? Recall the rule. A low clearance sign means you must not go on if your vehicle is taller than the height shown, or it may become stuck. So you do not continue under the structure. Find another route that avoids the low clearance. A narrow bridge sign is a different warning, telling you the bridge ahead is narrower than the road leading to it, so slow down there. Put simply: A narrow bridge sign means the bridge ahead is narrower than the road leading to it.

To sum up, crossing signs warn of animals, people or vehicles crossing, slippery road signs warn of wet surfaces and are often near bridges and overpasses, and steep hill signs mean check your brakes before going on. At a lane ends sign the ending lane yields and merges; at a merging traffic sign you make room; at an added lane sign no one needs to merge. A low clearance sign means do not go on if your vehicle is taller than shown, and a narrow bridge sign means the bridge is narrower than the road leading to it. Remember this rule: Crossing signs warn you to watch for animals, people or vehicles crossing the road.

why_how.text: Orange work zone signs and devices protect workers, and guide signs help you find your way.
Breaking the work zone limit while workers are present brings a fine.

scenario.text: In a work zone with a reduced limit posted, Eli sees crews working beside the road.

reasoning.text: Drivers who break the posted work zone speed limit while workers are present are fined three hundred dollars.

result.text: Eli slows to the posted work zone limit and shifts his lane position away from the crew.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking cones and barriers matter but the people holding signs are optional to follow.

correction.text: You must always follow people directing traffic with orange signs, flags or stop signs in work zones.

prompt.text: You need gas on a long trip. Which color of guide sign do you look for?

answer.text: Blue, the color of motorist services such as gas, food and rest areas.

rationale.text: Blue is the service color, while green shows exits and routes and brown shows points of interest.

narration.text: This unit covers two kinds of signs. The first are construction signs and devices: orange signs with black letters, drums, cones, tubes, flashing arrows and striped barriers, and the people who direct traffic in work zones. The second are guide signs, the brown, blue and green signs and route markers that help you find places, services and directions. Work zone signs ask you to slow down and follow directions to protect the people working there, while guide signs help you plan where you are going. Both are part of reading the road well.

Orange signs with black letters mark construction and work zones, warning of restricted lanes, detours and other road work hazards, and you should slow down when you see one. Drums, cones, tubes, flashing arrows and orange-and-white striped barriers keep traffic out of dangerous work areas, and you must always follow people directing traffic with orange signs, flags or stop signs. A flagger sign means a person with a flag is ahead, so drive cautiously. Treat every orange sign as a signal that the road ahead may not match what you expect.

lines.text: Road work sign: slow and shift away

narration.text: A road work sign showing workers means maintenance is under way, so slow down and shift your lane position to keep away from them. Reduced speed limits are often posted in work zones. Drivers who break the posted work zone speed limit while workers are present are fined three hundred dollars. So the work zone rules combine a lower speed, more space between you and the crew, and a real penalty for ignoring them. When you see workers beside the lane, ease off, move as far from them as your lane allows, and keep to the posted limit.

lines.text: People directing traffic must be obeyed

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers watch the cones and barriers carefully but treat the person holding a sign or flag, as a suggestion. That is wrong. Drums, cones, tubes, flashing arrows and orange-and-white striped barriers keep traffic out of dangerous work areas, and you must always follow people directing traffic with orange signs, flags or stop signs. A flagger's sign or signal carries the same weight as a traffic control device. When a flagger tells you to stop, you stop, and when the flagger tells you to go, you go carefully.

Brown signs point out historic sites, parks and other points of interest. Blue signs lead you to motorist services such as telephones, gas, food, motels, hospitals and rest areas. Green signs show exits, distances to cities, interstate interchanges, street or route names and bicycle routes. Route signs identify the type of road, with separate markers for interstate freeways, U.S. highways, Minnesota highways and county roads. Knowing which color carries which kind of information lets you scan quickly for what you need, whether that is gas, an exit or a park.

Here is a quick check: what do blue signs lead you to? Recall the guide sign colors. Blue signs lead you to motorist services such as telephones, gas, food, motels, hospitals and rest areas. Green signs show exits, distances to cities, interchanges, route names and bicycle routes, and brown signs point out historic sites, parks and other points of interest. So the answer is motorist services. When you need gas or a rest area on a long trip, look for the blue signs, and use the green ones to find your exit. Once more: Brown signs point out historic sites, parks and other points of interest.

lines.text: Brown sights, blue services, green guidance

narration.text: To wrap up, orange signs with black letters mark work zones, warning of restricted lanes, detours and hazards, so slow down. Drums, cones, tubes, flashing arrows and striped barriers keep traffic out, and you must always follow people directing traffic with signs or flags. Flagger and road work signs mean drive cautiously and shift away from workers, reduced limits are often posted, and breaking the limit while workers are present brings a three hundred dollar fine. Brown signs point to sights, blue to services, green to exits and routes, and route markers show the type of road.

why_how.text: Traffic signals keep busy intersections orderly, and two rules cover what to do when they fail or traffic backs up.

scenario.text: Kai's light turns green, but the cars beyond the intersection are stopped and there is no room for him on the far side.

reasoning.text: Do not enter an intersection with a traffic signal unless you can move through it immediately, continuously and completely without blocking cross traffic.

result.text: Kai waits behind the stop line until there is room to clear the intersection.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a dark traffic signal as if it were green.

correction.text: When a traffic signal is not working, treat the intersection as an uncontrolled intersection.

memory_support.text: Dark signal means uncontrolled; never enter what you cannot clear.

prompt.text: An officer waves you into an intersection you cannot clear. Does the gridlock rule stop you?

answer.text: No; the rule does not apply when a traffic-control agent or peace officer directs you.

rationale.text: Outside those cases, you may not enter a signal intersection you cannot clear.

title.text: When signals fail or traffic jams

narration.text: Traffic-control signals are placed at busy intersections to promote safety and orderly traffic flow. This short unit covers what happens when that order breaks down. You will learn how to treat an intersection when its signal is not working, and the gridlock rule, which keeps drivers from blocking an intersection when traffic beyond it is backed up. You will also learn the exceptions to the gridlock rule. These situations happen in every busy town, and handling them correctly keeps traffic moving for everyone instead of locking an intersection in place.

Traffic-control signals are placed at busy intersections to promote safety and orderly traffic flow. When a traffic signal is not working, treat the intersection as an uncontrolled intersection. That means the yielding rules for uncontrolled intersections apply, and no driver has a green light. Approach slowly, be ready to stop, and take turns with the other drivers using those rules. A dark signal does not give anyone the right to drive straight through, and treating it as uncontrolled keeps traffic from every direction moving safely.

lines.text: Enter only if you can clear

narration.text: Do not enter an intersection with a traffic signal unless you can move through it immediately, continuously and completely without blocking cross traffic. In other words, a green light is not enough on its own. If the traffic beyond the intersection is stopped and you would end up sitting in the middle when the light changes, you must wait behind the stop line. Entering anyway would leave you blocking cross traffic, which is exactly what the rule forbids. Wait for room on the far side, then go. To restate the key point: Do not enter an intersection with a traffic signal unless you can move through it immediately, continuously and completely without blocking cross traffic.

lines.text: Directed by an agent or officer
Moving aside for an emergency vehicle

narration.text: Here is the trap. The gridlock rule is strict, but it has three exceptions. The gridlock rule does not apply when a traffic-control agent or peace officer directs you, when you are moving aside for an emergency vehicle with lights on, or when your turn lets you leave the intersection safely. So if an officer waves you in, if you must clear a path for an emergency vehicle, or if you are making a turn that takes you out of the intersection, you may proceed. Outside those cases, do not enter unless you can clear it. Put simply: Do not enter an intersection with a traffic signal unless you can move through it immediately, continuously and completely without blocking cross traffic.

Here is a quick check: when does the gridlock rule not apply? Recall the three exceptions. The rule does not apply when a traffic-control agent or peace officer directs you, when you are moving aside for an emergency vehicle with its lights on, or when your turn lets you leave the intersection safely. In every other case, do not enter an intersection with a traffic signal unless you can move through it immediately, continuously and completely without blocking cross traffic. Knowing both the rule and its exceptions is what this topic tests.

To finish, traffic-control signals are placed at busy intersections to promote safety and orderly traffic flow. When a signal is not working, treat the intersection as an uncontrolled intersection. Do not enter a signal intersection unless you can move through it immediately, continuously and completely without blocking cross traffic. The gridlock rule does not apply when an agent or officer directs you, when you move aside for an emergency vehicle with lights on, or when your turn lets you leave the intersection safely. That completes the signs portion of this chapter.
